parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I plan and run flights for my drone operating company, deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off on flights before they leave. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight if needed. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether a load is ready, how the drone reaches its job points, and when it arrives.
The question: How do those jobs first reach you when you start your shift?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who do you interact with—who hands work to you, and who do you hand work off to during the day?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Could you give me an example of what happens when several of you are trying to plan for the same drone or busy site at the same time?

Q5
The answer just before it: Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. That worries me when we are trying to plan for those same busy sites and popular drones simultaneously.
The question: Tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months—what happened, and what made it so bad?

Q6
The answer just before it: Radio coverage was patchy in bad weather and around industrial sites, meaning reports from drones arrived late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Drones sometimes restarted in flight after a software fault and carried on, while closures were amended during the day and could even come into force while drones from several companies were already in the air. Batteries also drained faster in cold and wind than planned, and the server was updated and restarted during working hours while drones were flying, occasionally crashing.
The question: When something goes wrong like that—whether a flight problem or a server crash—what is the very first thing you need to know right afterward?

Q7
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking about that bad day, when an airspace closure came into force while your drones were already in the air, how did you find out and what did you have to do?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What things do you check by hand today before or during a flight because you don't fully trust the current information?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When we build a new service for your work, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

Q10
The answer just before it: I worry about a server crash, since the service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and the platform company accepts a few minutes of interruption. I am also concerned that closures can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and that closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.
The question: Before you sign off on a flight to leave, what information do you look at to decide which drone to use and which way it should go?

Q11
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, but software never chooses a drone or a way for us.
The question: What makes a drone suitable or able to get to where a job starts?

Q12
The answer just before it: Drones differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry like cameras, thermal cameras, or laser scanners, and which charging connector they use. Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company.
The question: What kinds of jobs are you planning flights for, and how do their routes or job points differ?

Q13
The answer just before it: I plan deliveries that carry a load from one site to another, and inspections that take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order before bringing it back to the starting point. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have a limited number of places where drones can take off and land at the same time.
The question: What determines when you need to call off a flight, either before it leaves or while it is in the air?

Q14
The answer just before it: I can call off a flight, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. Beyond that, I don't know.
The question: Earlier you mentioned things happening outside your control, like whether a load is ready—how do you find out when a load is ready or when a drone reaches its job points?

Q15
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: How do fleet technicians or the airspace desk come into your work, if at all?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What happens when a drone finishes a flight at a site that isn't its home site?

Q17
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Besides closures, what else affects the corridors or sites when you are deciding which way a drone should fly?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What do the reports coming from the drones actually tell you while a flight is underway?

Q19
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: How do you handle privacy or confidentiality regarding your company's flights, sites, and problems compared to the other companies using the platform?

Q20
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
The question: Are there any rules or requirements around keeping records of who signed off on a flight or called one off?

Q21
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What else about drones, charging pads, corridors, or planning flights haven't we touched on yet that is important for your daily work?

Q22
The answer just before it: Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.
The question: Is there anything else about airspace closures, temporary restrictions, or how you monitor ongoing flights that you want to make sure isn't missed?

Q23
The answer just before it: The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves, and they can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
The question: Thinking about the drones themselves—their maintenance, availability, or states—is there anything else a dispatcher needs to be aware of when choosing a drone?

Q24
The answer just before it: Drones are of several models from different manufacturers, and each company may run a few hundred of them. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
The question: Thinking about the sites, takeoff and landing places, and corridors, is there any other detail about how they are set up or shared?

Q25
The answer just before it: Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company.
The question: Is there anything else at all about your job, your company's needs, or the operating environment that we haven't covered yet?

Q26
The answer just before it: Radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, which causes reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are also unreliable, so an instruction may get through twice without the sender knowing if the first attempt arrived. Furthermore, nobody watches every drone at every moment, and one person may be responsible for hundreds.
The question: Because one person may be responsible for hundreds of drones and nobody watches every drone at every moment, what draws your attention to a particular flight?
